text:
jen_ae: quick heads-up — AtlasBank (payments) asking for a Private deployment POC. Requirements: no public ingress into their VPC, all outbound must be allowlisted to a short set of static IPs, and their security ops want original client IPs in logs. They asked us to recommend PrivateLink vs TGW/Peering, NAT/EIP approach, exact firewall lines, and a back-of-envelope cost delta vs Dedicated to scoping.

sam_se: thanks — couple clarifying Qs for the presales: multi-account or single account today? steady rps and burst? any mandatory mutual-TLS or specific cert requirements?

sam_se: also ask if they require long-term fixed IPs or are they ok with a weekly rotation cadence.

jen_ae: single AWS account for now, likely multi-account later. Steady ~80 rps, bursts to ~700 during batch windows. PCI + SOC2 in play; they require KMS + CloudTrail retention. They prefer fixed EIPs for downstream partner allowlists.

kraig_arch: top-line guidance: PrivateLink (NLB + VPCE) is the lower-risk path for "no public ingress" and generally faster security signoff. TGW/Peering (or dedicated ENIs in their subnets) is better for low-latency, high-throughput integrations or when they want our nodes reachable from many subnets. TGW is easier than peering when multi-account is required.

kraig_arch: tradeoffs in bullets:
- PrivateLink: pros — no route table edits, per-service VPCE, easier audit + minimal network blast radius. cons — per-region VPCEs, no transitive routing, NLB healthcheck ports must be allowed.
- TGW/Peering: pros — L3 connectivity, single routing plane for many services, lower per-packet latency. cons — CIDR planning, potential for overlapping IPs, longer security review.

priya_netops: on preserving original client IPs — three practical patterns we use:
1) Customer-managed egress forward proxy (recommended): a tiny NGINX/HAProxy box in their VPC with an EIP. We send traffic to that proxy (via PrivateLink or TGW), proxy forwards outbound and inserts X-Forwarded-For / X-Real-IP. On-prem IDS sees proxy EIP but logs contain original client IP in header.
2) Run nodes in their account + egress from their NAT GW: original IPs are not preserved by NAT; you lose L3 source unless you do advanced route engineering.
3) BGP/VPN with return-route advertisement: can preserve L2/L3 visibility but operationally complex and fragile for a POC.

priya_netops: firewall copy/paste block to give them:

```
# AtlasBank firewall egress snippet for Redwood POC
- Protocol: TCP
- Ports: 443
- Destination: <VPCE subnet CIDR or VPCE private IPs> OR <Redwood EIP set: 198.51.100.10,198.51.100.11>
- Description: Redwood Inference private endpoints / egress
# If NLB healthchecks are used, allow TCP 8443 (or confirm exact healthcheck port) from Redwood control-plane IPs to target hosts.
```

kraig_arch: TLS inspection note: if AtlasBank does TLS interception, advise they either:
- allow SNI for our hostnames, or
- use TLS passthrough on the VPCE/NLB path. Mutual TLS on control-plane APIs requires cert exchange ahead of time.

sam_se: what about the static EIPs ask? can we reserve EIPs on our side or do they need to provide them?

kraig_arch: options:
- Customer provides outbound EIP(s) on their side and hosts the small egress proxy — simplest for their auditing and downstream allowlists.
- Redwood can reserve and publish a small EIP set, but that triggers procurement and formal agreement (and ops cadence for publication/rotation).

priya_netops: operationally for POCs we often recommend the customer-run proxy pattern. It keeps control with them, preserves headers, and avoids us needing to manage dedicated EIPs in their firewall.

sam_se: quick firewall port question — apart from 443 any other ports we might ask them to open?

kraig_arch: generally just 443. If using NLB + VPCE we may need a healthcheck port (we commonly use 8443 or a TCP health port). If agent/control-plane requires metrics or sidecar callbacks, ops will confirm specific IPs and ports. I would include a caveat line in the questionnaire: "Allow TCP 8443 from Redwood control-plane IPs for healthchecks (confirm exact list with ops)."

sam_se: ballpark pricing for scoping (NOT a quote):
- Dedicated: predictable monthly commit — example for this workload (depending on model & batching) assume a 4-GPU reserved pool ~ $9k-12k/month; an 8-GPU pool ~ $18k-22k/month.
- Private (customer infra): Redwood platform onboarding fee ~$20k-$40k one-time + annual platform support ~$8k-$15k. Customer pays EC2/GPU/NAT/EIP in their account. Exact quote via finance.

jen_ae: blockers to surface in presales call?

kraig_arch: checklist to flag:
- overlapping CIDRs if TGW/peering is chosen — ask for their full VPC/subnet CIDR list early.
- strict egress policies that forbid any IP updates — we'll need an ops cadence for IP roll forward if necessary.
- requirement for air-gapped control plane or customer-managed control plane — that's a separate offering and impacts cost/timeline.

priya_netops: also confirm KMS/HSM expectations and CloudTrail/log retention windows. SIEM integration for trace/token-level logs is possible but requires policy review.

quotes-bot: reminder: for a formal quote, add finance contact and selected support tier; include whether they want a managed control-plane option.

jen_ae: next steps: I'll schedule a 30-minute tech handoff with AtlasBank + their netops for tomorrow 11am PT. @kraig_arch @priya_netops can you join? I'll ask AtlasBank to provide their proposed static EIP list and full VPC CIDRs before the call and will attach their security questionnaire.

kraig_arch: I can join.

priya_netops: available.

jen_ae: thanks everyone — I'll post updates after the handoff. :thumbsup:
